entries.30d00533725b5dd5ade551f6d08ac2b0ea63234a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5393"/><div sID="gen8108" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5393"/><hi type="bold">11. rage--</hi>rather, pour out the redundant floods of, &c.<div eID="gen8108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8109" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">behold--</hi>Try, canst thou, as God, by a mere glance abase the proud (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.12">Is 2:12</reference>, &c.)? <div eID="gen8109" type="x-p"/>
entries.144873ae54a399e8ff2bebb94e5fe5d85de19424: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5394"/><div sID="gen8110" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5394"/><hi type="bold">12. proud--</hi>high (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.37">Da 4:37</reference>).<div eID="gen8110" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8111" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in their place--</hi>on the spot; suddenly, before they can move from their place. (See on <reference osisRef="Job.34.26">Job 34:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.36.20">Job 36:20</reference>). <div eID="gen8111" type="x-p"/>
entries.dc2eb2bbda52b8b40f397b7b034d1d221c8206fb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5395"/><div sID="gen8112" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5395"/>13. (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.10">Is 2:10</reference>). Abase and remove them out of the sight of men.<div eID="gen8112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8113" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bind ... faces--</hi>that is, shut up their persons [Maurer]. But it refers rather to the custom of binding a cloth over the faces of persons about to be executed (<reference osisRef="Job.9.24">Job 9:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Esth.7.8">Es 7:8</reference>).<div eID="gen8113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8114" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in secret--</hi>consign them to darkness. <div eID="gen8114" type="x-p"/>
entries.32469fe8ce0398eb5e0272b263339e24e068cb5c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5396"/><div sID="gen8115" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5396"/><hi type="bold">14. confess--</hi>rather, "extol"; "I also," who now censure thee. But since thou canst not do these works, thou must, instead of censuring, extol My government.<div eID="gen8115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8116" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thine own ... hand ... save--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.44.3">Psa 44:3</reference>). So as to eternal salvation by Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="Isa.59.16">Is 59:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.63.5">63:5</reference>). <div eID="gen8116" type="x-p"/>
entries.5f30cf277229b4f4d659ad0c94511dca73c991b1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5397"/><div sID="gen8117" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5397"/>15-24. God shows that if Job cannot bring under control the lower animals (of which he selects the two most striking, behemoth on land, leviathan in the water), much less is he capable of governing the world.<div eID="gen8117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8118" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">behemoth--</hi>The description in part agrees with the hippopotamus, in part with the elephant, but exactly in all details with neither. It is rather a poetical personification of the great Pachydermata, or Herbivora (so "he eateth grass"), the idea of the hippopotamus being predominant. In <reference osisRef="Job.40.17">Job 40:17</reference>, "the tail like a cedar," hardly applies to the latter (so also <reference osisRef="Job.40.20">Job 40:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.40.23">23</reference>, "Jordan," a river which elephants alone could reach, but see on <reference osisRef="Job.40.23">Job 40:23</reference>). On the other hand, <reference osisRef="Job.40.21">Job 40:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.40.22">22</reference> are characteristic of the amphibious river horse. So leviathan (the twisting animal), <reference osisRef="Job.41.1">Job 41:1</reference>, is a generalized term for cetacea, pythons, saurians of the neighboring seas and rivers, including the crocodile, which is the most prominent, and is often associated with the river horse by old writers. "Behemoth" seems to be the Egyptian Pehemout, "water-ox," Hebraized, so-called as being like an ox, whence the Italian bombarino.<div eID="gen8118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8119" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with thee--</hi>as I made thyself. Yet how great the difference! The manifold wisdom and power of God!<div eID="gen8119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8120" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he eateth grass--</hi>marvellous in an animal living so much in the water; also strange, that such a monster should not be carnivorous. <div eID="gen8120" type="x-p"/>

entries.1130a508ceff21940e4b3e161025a84044f3e450: <div eID="gen18068" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen18069" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen18070" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18070" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18069" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen18071" type="x-p"/> Job humbles himself before the Lord, <reference osisRef="Job.40.1-Job.40.5">Job 40:1-5</reference>. And God again challenges him by a display of his power and judgments, <reference osisRef="Job.40.6-Job.40.14">Job 40:6-14</reference>. A description of behemoth, <reference osisRef="Job.40.15-Job.40.24">Job 40:15-24</reference>. <div eID="gen18071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18072" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen18072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18073" type="x-p"/> Moreover the Lord answered - That is, the Lord continued his discourse with Job. Answered does not refer to any thing said by Job, or any question asked. I think it very likely that this whole piece, from the beginning of this first verse to the end of the fourteenth, was originally the ending of the poem. Mr. Heath has noticed this, and I shall lay his words before the reader: "The former part of this chapter is evidently the conclusion of the poem; the latter part whereof seems to be in great disorder; whether it has happened from the carelessness of the transcriber, or, which appears most probable, from the skins of parchment composing the roll having by some accident changed their places. It is plain from the seventh verse of the forty-second chapter (<reference osisRef="Job.42.7">Job 42:7</reference>) that Jehovah is the last speaker in the poem. If, then, immediately after the end of the thirty-ninth chapter, we subjoin the fifteenth verse of the forty-second chapter, and place the fourteen first verses of the fortieth chapter immediately after the sixth verse of the forty-second chapter, and by that means make them the conclusion of the poem, all will be right; and this seventh verse of the forty-second chapter will be in its natural order. The action will be complete by the judgment of the Almighty; and the catastrophe of the poem will be grand and solemn." To these reasons of Mr. Heath, Dr. Kennicott has added others, which the reader may find at the end of the chapter. (<reference osisRef="Job.40.24">Job 40:24</reference>) Without taking any farther notice of the transposition in this place, I will continue the notes in the present order of the verses.
entries.57354ae0c0f24433cf55e563a708ce27f8d2a2c7: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen18073" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18074" type="x-p"/> He that reproveth God, let him answer it - Let the man who has made so free with God and his government, answer to what he has now heard.
entries.c8e4bdbc41cea121308d3e3e1ca277bc09a12556: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen18074" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18075" type="x-p"/> Behold, I am vile - I acknowledge my inward defilement. I cannot answer thee. <div eID="gen18075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18076" type="x-p"/> I will lay mine hand upon my mouth - I cannot excuse myself, and I must be dumb before thee.
entries.709734cad3c9313171c680f9c1d88c56932b98cb: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen18076" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18077" type="x-p"/> Once have I spoken - See on <reference osisRef="Job.42.3">Job 42:3</reference> (note), etc. <div eID="gen18077" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18078" type="x-p"/> I will proceed no farther - I shall attempt to justify myself no longer; I have spoken repeatedly; and am confounded at my want of respect for my Maker, and at the high thoughts which I have entertained of my own righteousness. All is impurity in the presence of thy Majesty.
entries.2bd58035f4e919d511c6645f5ba5c4c35fee6668: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen18078" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18079" type="x-p"/> Gird up thy loins - See <reference osisRef="Job.38.1-Job.38.3">Job 38:1-3</reference>. Some think that this and the preceding verse have been repeated here from <reference osisRef="Job.38.1-Job.38.3">Job 38:1-3</reference>, and that several of the words there, here, and <reference osisRef="Job.42.3">Job 42:3</reference>, have been repeated, in after times, to connect some false gatherings of the sheets of parchment, on which the end of this poem was originally written. See on <reference osisRef="Job.40.1">Job 40:1</reference> (note), and at the end of the chapter.
entries.ffa05c0b3889843a99446dfce94fc242b764a00c: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen18079" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18080" type="x-p"/> Wilt thou condemn me - Rather than submit to be thought in the wrong, wilt thou condemn My conduct, in order to justify thyself? Some men will never acknowledge themselves in the wrong. "God may err, but we cannot," seems to be their impious maxim. Unwillingness to acknowledge a fault frequently leads men, directly or indirectly, to this sort of blasphemy. There are three words most difficult to be pronounced in all languages, - I Am Wrong.
entries.05744df3b28a415ecc138e32fee975f4c945ddce: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen18080" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18081" type="x-p"/> Hast thou an arm like God? - Every word, from this to the end of <reference osisRef="Job.40.14">Job 40:14</reference>, has a wonderful tendency to humble the soul; and it is no wonder that at the conclusion of these sayings Job fell in the dust confounded, and ascribed righteousness to his Maker.
entries.0f8b5b0e5be27ffb058fec6cdab6ed0003cf43d6: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen18081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18082" type="x-p"/> Deck thyself now with majesty - Act like God, seeing thou hast been assuming to thyself perfections that belong to him alone.
entries.b4c789c49a2b03b9feb7826686f9a70d8cf96f09: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen18082" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18083" type="x-p"/> Hide them in the dust together - Blend the high and the low, the rich and the poor, in one common ruin. Show them that thou art supreme, and canst do whatsoever thou pleasest. <div eID="gen18083" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18084" type="x-p"/> Bind their faces in secret - This seems to refer to the custom of preserving mummies: the whole body is wrapped round with strong swathings of linen or cotton cloth. Not only the limbs, but the very head, face, and all, are rolled round with strong filleting, so that not one feature can be seen, not even the protuberance of the nose. On the outside of these involutions a human face is ordinarily painted; but as to the real face itself, it is emphatically bound in secret, for those rollers are never intended to be removed.
entries.efd4dd1ecf6c700569519adf766b7187323fa16f: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen18084" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18085" type="x-p"/> Thine own right hand can save thee - It is the prerogative of God alone to save the human soul. Nothing less than unlimited power, exerted under the direction and impulse of unbounded mercy, can save a sinner. This is most clearly asserted in this speech of Jehovah: When thou canst extend an arm like God, i.e., an uncontrollable power - when thou canst arm thyself with the lightning of heaven, and thunder with a voice like God - when thou canst deck thyself with the ineffable glory, beauty, and splendor of the supreme majesty of Jehovah - when thou canst dispense thy judgments over all the earth, to abase the proud, and tread down the wicked - when thou canst as having the keys of hell and death, blend the high and the low in the dust together; then I will acknowledge to thee that thy own right hand can save thee. In other words: Salvation belongeth unto the Lord; no man can save his own soul by works of righteousness which he has done, is doing, or can possibly do, to all eternity. Without Jesus every human spirit must have perished everlastingly. Glory be to God for his unspeakable gift!
entries.0c26fa2eb12ab0614e26e876cd32b440be4849b5: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen18085" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18086" type="x-p"/> Behold now behemoth - The word בהמות behemoth is the plural of בהמה behemah, which signifies cattle in general, or graminivorous animals, as distinguished from חיתו chayetho, all wild or carnivorous animals. See <reference osisRef="Gen.1.24">Gen 1:24</reference>. The former seems to mean kine, horses, asses, sheep, etc., and all employed in domestic or agricultural matters; the latter, all wild and savage beasts, such as lions, bears, tigers, etc.: but the words are not always taken in these senses. <div eID="gen18086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18087" type="x-p"/> In this place it has been supposed to mean some animal of the beeve kind. The Vulgate retains the Hebrew name; so do the Syriac and Arabic. The Chaldee is indefinite, translating creature or animal. And the Septuagint is not more explicit, translating by θηρια, beasts or wild beasts; and old Coverdale, the cruell beaste, perhaps as near to the truth as any of them. From the name, therefore, or the understanding had of it by the ancient versions, we can derive no assistance relative to the individuality of the animal in question; and can only hope to find what it is by the characteristics it bears in the description here given of it. <div eID="gen18087" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18088" type="x-p"/> These, having been carefully considered and deeply investigated both by critics and naturalists, have led to the conclusion that either the elephant, or the hippopotamus or river-horse, is the animal in question; and on comparing the characteristics between these two, the balance is considerably in favor of the hippopotamus. But even here there are still some difficulties, as there are some parts of the description which do not well suit even the hippopotamus; and therefore I have my doubts whether either of the animals above is that in question, or whether any animal now in existence be that described by the Almighty. <div eID="gen18088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18089" type="x-p"/> Mr. Good supposes, and I am of the same opinion, that the animal here described is now extinct. The skeletons of three lost genera have actually been found out: these have been termed palaeotherium, anoplotherium, and mastodon or mammoth. From an actual examination of a part of the skeleton of what is termed the mammoth, I have described it in my note on <reference osisRef="Gen.1.24">Gen 1:24</reference>. <div eID="gen18089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18090" type="x-p"/> As I do not believe that either the elephant or the river-horse is intended here, I shall not take up the reader's time with any detailed description. The elephant is well known; and, though not an inhabitant of these countries, has been so often imported in a tame state, and so frequently occurs in exhibitions of wild beasts, that multitudes, even of the common people, have seen this tremendous, docile, and sagacious animal. Of the hippopotamus or river-horse, little is generally known but by description, as the habits of this animal will not permit him to be tamed. His amphibious nature prevents his becoming a constant resident on dry land. <div eID="gen18090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18091" type="x-p"/> The hippopotamus inhabits the rivers of Africa and the lakes of Ethiopia: feeds generally by night; wanders only a few miles from water; feeds on vegetables and roots of trees, but never on fish; lays waste whole plantations of the sugar-cane, rice, and other grain. When irritated or wounded, it will attack boats and men with much fury. It moves slowly and heavily: swims dexterously; walks deliberately and leisurely over head into the water; and pursues his way, even on all fours, on the bottom; but cannot remain long under the water without rising to take in air. It sleeps in reedy places; has a tremendous voice, between the lowing of an ox and the roaring of the elephant. Its head is large; its mouth, very wide; its skin, thick and almost devoid of hair; and its tail, naked and about a foot long. It is nearly as large as the elephant, and some have been found seventeen feet long. Mr. Good observes: "Both the elephant and hippopotamus are naturally quiet animals; and never interfere with the grazing of others of different kinds unless they be irritated. The behemoth, on the contrary, is represented as a quadruped of a ferocious nature, and formed for tyranny, if not rapacity; equally lord of the floods and of the mountains; rushing with rapidity of foot, instead of slowness or stateliness; and possessing a rigid and enormous tail, like a cedar tree, instead of a short naked tail of about a foot long, as the hippopotamus; or a weak, slender, hog-shaped tail, as the elephant." <div eID="gen18091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18092" type="x-p"/> The mammoth, for size, will answer the description in this place, especially <reference osisRef="Job.40.19">Job 40:19</reference> : He is the chief of the ways of God. That to which the part of a skeleton belonged which I examined, must have been, by computation, not less than twenty-five feet high, and sixty feet in length! The bones of one toe I measured, and found them three feet in length! One of the very smallest grinders of an animal of this extinct species, full of processes on the surface more than an inch in depth, which shows that the animal had lived on flesh, I have just now weighed, and found it, in its very dry state, four pounds eight ounces, avoirdupois: the same grinder of an elephant I have weighed also, and found it just two pounds. The mammoth, therefore, from this proportion, must have been as large as two elephants and a quarter. We may judge by this of its size: elephants are frequently ten and eleven feet high; this will make the mammoth at least twenty-five or twenty-six feet high; and as it appears to have been a many-toed animal, the springs which such a creature could make must have been almost incredible: nothing by swiftness could have escaped its pursuit. God seems to have made it as the proof of his power; and had it been prolific, and not become extinct, it would have depopulated the earth. Creatures of this kind must have been living in the days of Job; the behemoth is referred to here, as if perfectly and commonly known. <div eID="gen18092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18093" type="x-p"/> He eateth grass as an ox - This seems to be mentioned as something remarkable in this animal: that though from the form of his teeth he must have been carnivorous, yet he ate grass as an ox; he lived both on animal and vegetable food.
entries.8d7f9ed07174998122da48f34012e195af98c48b: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen18093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18094" type="x-p"/> His strength is in his loins - This refers to his great agility, notwithstanding his bulk; by the strength of his loins he was able to take vast springs, and make astonishing bounds.
entries.3288a31437151f552420c8c0481c6c3f586def3a: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen18094" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18095" type="x-p"/> He moveth his tail like a cedar - Therefore it was neither the elephant, who has a tail like that of the hog, nor the hippopotamus, whose tail is only about a foot long. <div eID="gen18095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18096" type="x-p"/> The sinews of his stones - I translate with Mr. Good, and for the same reasons, the sinews of his haunches, which is still more characteristic; as the animal must have excelled in leaping.
entries.cbe801f78bb0d75c64175648bbd543b0242592e1: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen18096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18097" type="x-p"/> His bones are as strong pieces of brass-bars of iron - The tusk I have mentioned above is uncommonly hard, solid, and weighty for its size.
entries.b45e6632a74cdea7855c3d3371bdd0cbc8a320bf: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen18097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18098" type="x-p"/> He is the chief of the ways of God - The largest, strongest, and swiftest quadruped that God has formed. <div eID="gen18098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18099" type="x-p"/> He that made him - No power of man or beast can overcome him. God alone can overcome him, and God alone could make his sword (of extinction) approach to him.
entries.9c0c18020e91bd7ced085218a29b7a2e29d65508: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen18099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18100" type="x-p"/> The mountains bring him forth food - It cannot therefore be the hippopotamus, as he is seldom found far from the rivers where he has his chief residence. <div eID="gen18100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18101" type="x-p"/> Where all the beasts of the field play - He frequents those places where he can have most prey. He makes a mock of all the beasts of the field. They can neither resist his power, nor escape from his agility. All this answers to what we know of the mammoth, but not at all to the hippopotamus.
entries.a6e081d664dc708d8fc2f08ab79bf55e6a56e41f: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen18101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18102" type="x-p"/> He lieth under the shady trees - This and the following verses refer to certain habits of the behemoth, with which we are and must be unacquainted,
entries.a842b1811ea2605ac36d7a7cd45e5f6b6a995efa: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen18102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18103" type="x-p"/> The willows of the brook compass him - This would agree well enough with the hippopotamus.
entries.cb7e264b99dae2ea99245b1e65e3d6531602ebe5: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen18103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18104" type="x-p"/> Behold, he drinketh up a river - A similar mode of expression, and of precisely the same meaning, as that in <reference osisRef="Job.39.24">Job 39:24</reference> : "He swalloweth the ground with fierceness." No river can stop his course: he wades through all; stems every tide and torrent; and hurries not as though he were in danger. <div eID="gen18104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18105" type="x-p"/> He trusteth that he can draw up Jordan - Even when the river overflows its banks, it is no stoppage to him: though the whole impetuosity of its stream rush against his mouth, he is not afraid. Mr. Good has seized the true idea in his translation of this verse: - "If the stream rage, he revileth not: <div eID="gen18105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18106" type="x-p"/> He is unmoved, though Jordan rush against his mouth." <div eID="gen18106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18107" type="x-p"/> From this mention of Jordan it is probable that the behemoth was once an inhabitant of the mountains, marshes, and woods, of the land of Palestine.
entries.7bf0a7d5b0f13dc688c001ce7e194a2ff01bca37: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen18107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18108" type="x-p"/> He taketh it with his eyes - He looks at the sweeping tide, and defies it. <div eID="gen18108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18109" type="x-p"/> His nose pierceth through snares - If fences of strong stakes be made in order to restrain him, or prevent him from passing certain boundaries, he tears them in pieces with his teeth; or, by pressing his nose against them, breaks them off. If other parts of the description would answer, this might well apply to the elephant, the nose here meaning the proboscis, with which he can split trees, or even tear them up from the roots! Thus ends the description of the behemoth; what I suppose to be the mastodon or mammoth, or some creature of this kind, that God made as the chief of his works, exhibited in various countries for a time, cut them off from the earth, but by his providence preserved many of their skeletons, that succeeding ages might behold the mighty power which produced this chief of the ways of God, and admire the providence that rendered that race extinct which would otherwise, in all probability, have extinguished every other race of animals! I am not unapprized of the strong arguments produced by learned men to prove, on the one hand, that behemoth is the elephant; and, on the other, that he is the hippopotamus or river-horse, and I have carefully read all that Bochart, that chief of learned men, has said on the subject. But I am convinced that an animal now extinct, probably of the kind already mentioned, is the creature pointed out and described by the inspiration of God in this chapter. <div eID="gen18109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18110" type="x-p"/> On <reference osisRef="Job.40.1">Job 40:1</reference> of this chapter we have seen, from Mr. Heath's remarks, that the fourteen first verses were probably transposed. In the following observations Dr. Kennicott appears to prove the point. "It will be here objected, that the poem could not possibly end with this question from Job; and, among other reasons, for this in particular; because we read in the very next verse, That after the Lord had spoken these words unto Job, etc. If, therefore, the last speaker was not Job, but the Lord, Job could not originally have concluded this poem, as he does at present. "This objection I hold to be exceedingly important; and, indeed, to prove decisively that the poem must have ended at first with some speech from God. "And this remark leads directly to a very interesting inquiry: What was at first the conclusion of this poem? This may, I presume, be pointed out and determined, not by the alteration of any one word, but only by allowing a dislocation of the fourteen verses which now begin the fortieth chapter. Chapters 38, 39, 40, and 41, contain a magnificent display of the Divine power and wisdom in the works of the Creator; specifying the lion, raven, wild goat, wild ass, unicorn, peacock, ostrich, horse, hawk, eagle, behemoth, and leviathan. "Now, it must have surprised most readers to find that the description of these creatures is strangely interrupted at <reference osisRef="Job.40.1">Job 40:1</reference>, and as strangely resumed afterwards at <reference osisRef="Job.40.15">Job 40:15</reference>; and therefore, if these fourteen verses will connect with and regularly follow what now ends the poem, we cannot much doubt that these fourteen verses have again found their true station, and should be restored to it. "The greatness of the supposed transposition is no objection: because so many verses as would fill one piece of vellum in an ancient roll, might be easily sewed in before or after its proper place. In the case before us, the twenty-five lines in the first fourteen verses of chapter xl. seem to have been sewed in improperly after <reference osisRef="Job.39.30">Job 39:30</reference>, instead of after <reference osisRef="Job.42.6">Job 42:6</reference>. That such large parts have been transposed in rolls to make which the parts are sewed together is absolutely certain; and that this has been the case here, is still more probable for the following reason: - "The lines here supposed to be out of place are twenty-five, and contain ninety-two words; which might be written on one piece or page of vellum. But the MS. in which these twenty-five lines made one page, must be supposed to have the same, or nearly the same, number of lines in each of the pages adjoining. And it would greatly strengthen this presumption if these twenty-five lines would fall in regularly at the end of any other set of lines, nearly of the same number; if they would fall in after the next set of twenty-five, or the second set, or the third, or the fourth, etc. Now, this is actually the case here; for the lines after these twenty-five, being one hundred or one hundred and one, make just four times twenty-five. And, therefore, if we consider these one hundred and twenty-five lines as written on five equal pieces of vellum, it follows that the fifth piece might be carelessly sewed up before the other four. "Let us also observe that present disorder of the speeches, which is this. In chapters 38 and 39, God first speaks to Job. The end of chapter 39 is followed by, 'And the Lord answered Job and said,' whilst yet Job had not replied. At <reference osisRef="Job.40.3-Job.40.5">Job 40:3-5</reference>, Job answers; but he says, he had then spoken Twice, and he would add no more; whereas, this was his first reply, and he speaks afterwards. From Job 40:15-41:34 are now the descriptions of behemoth and leviathan, which would regularly follow the descriptions of the horse, hawk, and eagle. And from <reference osisRef="Job.42.1-Job.42.6">Job 42:1-6</reference> is now Job's speech, after which we read in <reference osisRef="Job.42.7">Job 42:7</reference>, 'After the Lord had spoken these words unto Job!' "Now, all these confusions are removed at once if we only allow that a piece of vellum containing the twenty-five lines, (<reference osisRef="Job.40.1-Job.40.14">Job 40:1-14</reference>), originally followed <reference osisRef="Job.42.6">Job 42:6</reference>. For then, after God's first speech, ending with leviathan, Job replies: then God, to whom Job replies the second time, when he added no more; and then God addresses him the third, when Job is silent, and the poem concludes: upon which the narrative opens regularly, with saying, 'After the Lord had spoken these words unto Job,' etc. <reference osisRef="Job.42.7">Job 42:7</reference>." - Kennicott's Remarks, p. 161. The reader will find much more satisfaction if he read the places as above directed. Having ended chapter 29, proceed immediately to <reference osisRef="Job.40.15">Job 40:15</reference>; go on regularly to the end of <reference osisRef="Job.42.6">Job 42:6</reference>, and immediately after that add <reference osisRef="Job.40.1-Job.40.14">Job 40:1-14</reference>. We shall find then that the poem has a consistent and proper ending, and that the concluding speech was spoken by Jehovah.  <chapter eID="Job.40"/> <div eID="gen18110" type="x-p"/>

entries.82126081743712f47e45e3f75c2801a7f904de02: <reference osisRef="Job.40.1-Job.3.1">Job 40:1-3   1</reference>  Then Jehovah answered Job, and said:   2  Will now the censurer contend with the Almighty? <div eID="gen8709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8710" type="x-p"/> Let the instructor of Eloah answer it!   3  Then Job answered Jehovah, and said: <div eID="gen8710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8711" type="x-p"/> With <reference osisRef="Job.40.1">Job 40:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.38.1">Job 38:1</reference> is again taken up, because the speech of Jehovah has now in some measure attained the end which was assigned to it as an answer to Job’s outburst of censure. רב is <hi type="italic">inf. abs.,</hi> as Jdg 11:25; it is left to the hearer to give to the simple verbal notion its syntactic relation in accordance with the connection; here it stands in the sense of the <hi type="italic">fut</hi>. (comp. 2Ki 4:43): <hi type="italic">num litigabit</hi>, Ges. §131, 4, <hi type="italic">b</hi>. The <hi type="italic">inf. abs. </hi>is followed by יסּור as subj., which (after the form שׁכּור) signifies a censurer and fault-finder, moomeetee's. The question means, will Job persist in this contending with God? He who sets God right, as though he knew everything better than He, shall answer the questions put before him.
entries.f941faa77ac78e455e98cbb641c8621f9ace9553: <reference osisRef="Job.40.4-Job.5.4">Job 40:4-5   4</reference>  Behold, I am too mean: what shall I answer Thee? <div eID="gen8711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8712" type="x-p"/> I lay my hand upon my mouth.   5  Once have I spoken, and will not begin again; <div eID="gen8712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8713" type="x-p"/> And twice - I will do it no more. <div eID="gen8713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8714" type="x-p"/> He is small, i.e., not equal to the task imposed, therefore he keeps his mouth firmly closed (comp. <reference osisRef="Job.21.5">Job 21:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.29.9">Job 29:9</reference>), for whatever he might say would still not be to the point. Once he has dared to criticise God’s doings; a second time (שׁתּים = שׁנית, Ges. §120, 5) he ventures it no more, for God’s wondrous wisdom and all-careful love dazzle him, and he gladly bows. <div eID="gen8714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8715" type="x-p"/> But how? Is not the divine speech altogether different from what one ought to expect? One expects to hear from the mouth of Jehovah something unheard of in the previous course of the drama, and in this expectation we find ourselves disappointed at the outset. For one need only look back and read <reference osisRef="Job.9.4-Job.9.10">Job 9:4-10</reference>, where Job acknowledges and describes God as a wise and mighty Lord over the natural world, especially as an irresistible Ruler over everything great in it; <reference osisRef="Job.12.7-Job.12.10">Job 12:7-10</reference>, where he refers to the creatures of the sky and deep as proofs of God’s creative power; <reference osisRef="Job.12.11-Job.12.25">Job 12:11-25</reference>, where he sketches the grandest picture of God’s terrible doings in nature and among men; <reference osisRef="Job.26.5-Job.26.14">Job 26:5-14</reference>, where he praises God as the Creator and Lord of all things, and describes what he says concerning Him as only a faint echo of the thunder of His might; <reference osisRef="Job.28.23">Job 28:23</reference>, where he ascribes absolute wisdom to Him as the Creator of and Ruler of the world. If one ponders these passages of Job’s speeches, he will not be able to say that the speech of Jehovah, in the exhibition of the creative power and wisdom of God, which is its theme, would make Job conscious of anything which was previously unknown to him; and it is accordingly asked, What, then, is there that is new in the speech of Jehovah by which the great effect is brought about, that Job humbles himself in penitence, and becomes ready for the act of redemption which follows? <div eID="gen8715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8716" type="x-p"/> It has indeed never occurred to Job to desire to enter into a controversy with God concerning the works of creation; he is far from the delusion of being able to stand such a test; he knows in general, that if God were willing to contend with him, he would not be able to answer God one in a thousand, Job 9:3. And yet God closely questioned him, and thereby Job comes to the perception of his sin - how comes it to pass? Has the plot of the drama perhaps failed in this point? Has the poet made use of means unsuited to the connection of the whole, to bring about the needful effect, viz., the repentance of Job, - because, perhaps, the store of his thoughts was exhausted? But this poet is not so poor, and we shall therefore be obliged to try and understand the disposition of the speech of Jehovah before we censure it. <div eID="gen8716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8717" type="x-p"/> When one of Job’s last words before the appearing of Jehovah was the word שׁדי יענני, Job thereby desired God’s decision concerning the testimony of his innocence. This wish is in itself not sinful; yea, it is even a fruit of his hidden faith, when he casts the look of hope away from his affliction and the accusation of the friends, into the future to God as his Vindicator and Redeemer. But that wish becomes sinful when he looks upon his affliction as a <hi type="italic">de facto</hi> accusation on the part of God, because he cannot think of suffering and sin as separable, and because he is conscious of his innocence, looks upon it as a decree of God, his opponent and his enemy, which is irreconcilable with the divine justice. This Job’s condition of conflict and temptation is the prevailing one; his faith is beclouded, and breaks through the night which hangs over him only in single rays. The result of this condition of conflict is the sinful character which that wish assumes: it becomes a challenge to God, since Job directs against God Himself the accusation which the friends have directed against him, and asserts his ability to carry through his good cause even if God would enter with him into a judicial contention; he becomes a יסור and מוכיח אלוה, and raises himself above God, because he thinks he has Him for an enemy who is his best friend. This defiance is, however, not common godlessness; on the contrary, Job is really the innocent servant of God, and his defiant tone is only the result of a false conception which the tempted one indulges respecting the Author of his affliction. So, then, this defiance has not taken full possession of Job’s mind; on the contrary, the faith which lays firm hold on confidence in the God whom he does not comprehend, is in conflict against it; and this conflict tends in the course of the drama, the nearer it comes to the catastrophe, still nearer to the victory, which only awaits a decisive stroke in order to be complete. Therefore Jehovah yields to Job’s longing שׁדי יענני, in as far as He really answers Job; and even that this takes place, and that, although out of the storm, it nevertheless takes place, not in a way to crush and destroy, but to instruct and convince, and displaying a loving condescension, is an indirect manifestation that Job is not regarded by God as an evil-doer mature for judgment. But that folly and temerity by which the servant of God is become unlike himself must notwithstanding be destroyed; and before Job can realize God as his Witness and Redeemer, in which character his faith in the brighter moments has foreseen Him, his sinful censuring and blaming of God must be blotted out by penitence; and with it at the same time his foolish imagination, by which his faith has been almost overwhelmed, must be destroyed, viz., the imagination that his affliction is a <hi type="italic">hostile</hi> dispensation of God. <div eID="gen8717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8718" type="x-p"/> And by what means is Job brought to the penitent recognition of his gloomy judgment concerning the divine decree, and of his contending with God? Is it, perhaps, by God’s admitting to him what really is the case: that he does not suffer as a sinner the punishment of his sin, but showing at the same time that the decree of suffering is not an unjust one, because its design is not hostile? No, indeed, for Job is not worthy that his cause should be acknowledged on the part of God before he has come to a penitent recognition of the wrong by which he has sinned against God. God would be encouraging self-righteousness if He should give Job the testimony of his innocence, before the sin of vainglory, into which Job has fallen in the consciousness of his innocence, is changed to <hi type="italic">humility</hi>, by which all uprightness that is acceptable with God is tested. Therefore, contrary to expectation, God begins to speak with Job about totally different matters from His justice or injustice in reference to his affliction. Therein already lies a deep humiliation for Job. But a still deeper one in God’s turning, as it were, to the <hi type="italic">abecedarium naturae,</hi> and putting the censurer of His doings to the blush. That God is the almighty and all-wise Creator and Ruler of the world, that the natural world is exalted above human knowledge and power, and is full of marvellous divine creations and arrangements, full of things mysterious and incomprehensible to ignorant and feeble man, Job knows even before God speaks, and yet he must now hear it, because he does not know it rightly; for the nature with which he is acquainted as the herald of the creative and governing power of God, is also the preacher of humility; and exalted as God the Creator and Ruler of the natural world is above Job’s censure, so is He also as the Author of his affliction. That which is new, therefore, in the speech of Jehovah, is not the proof of God’s exaltation in itself, but the relation to the mystery of his affliction, and to his conduct towards God in this his affliction, in which Job is necessitated to place perceptions not in themselves strange to him. He who cannot answer a single one of those questions taken from the natural kingdom, but, on the contrary, must everywhere admire and adore the power and wisdom of God-he must appear as an insignificant fool, if he applies them to his limited judgment concerning the Author of his affliction. <div eID="gen8718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8719" type="x-p"/> The fundamental tone of the divine speech is the thought, that the divine working in nature is infinitely exalted above human knowledge and power, and that consequently man must renounce all claim to better knowledge and right of contention in the presence of the divine dispensations. But at the same time, within the range of this general thought, it is also in particular shown how nature reflects the goodness of God as well as His wisdom (He has restrained the destructive power of the waters, He also sendeth rain upon the steppe, though untenanted by man); how that which accomplishes the purposes for which it was in itself designed, serves higher purposes in the moral order of the world (the dawn of day puts an end to the works of darkness, snow and hail serve as instruments of divine judgments); how divine providence extends to all creatures, and always according to their need (He provides the lion its prey, He satisfies the ravens that cry to Him); and how He has distributed His manifold gifts in a way often paradoxical to man, but in truth worthy of admiration (to the steinbock ease in bringing forth and growth without toil, to the wild ass freedom, to the antelope untameable fleetness, to the ostrich freedom from anxiety about its young and swiftness, to the horse heroic and proud lust for the battle, to the hawk the instinct of migration, to the eagle a lofty nest and a piercing sight). Everywhere the wonders of God’s power and wisdom, and in fact of His goodness abounding in power, and His providence abounding in wisdom, infinitely transcend Job’s knowledge and capacity. Job cannot answer one of all these questions, but yet he feels to what end they are put to him. The God who sets bounds to the sea, who refreshes the desert, who feeds the ravens, who cares for the gazelle in the wilderness and the eagle in its eyrie, is the same God who now causes him seemingly thus unjustly to suffer. But if the former is worthy of adoration, the latter will also be so. Therefore Job confesses that he will henceforth keep silence, and solemnly promises that he will now no longer contend with Him. From the marvellous in nature he divines that which is marvellous in his affliction. His humiliation under the mysteries of nature is at the same time humiliation under the mystery of his affliction; and only now, when he penitently reveres the mystery he has hitherto censured, is it time that its inner glory should be unveiled to him. The bud is mature, and can now burst forth, in order to disclose the blended colours of its matured beauty.
entries.c4d6879941f3c411f30efb3f3da6f988cb089fa3: <reference osisRef="Job.40.6">Job 40:6</reference>   <reference osisRef="Job.40.6">6</reference>  Then Jehovah answered Job out of the storm, and said: <div eID="gen8719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8720" type="x-p"/> This second time also Jehovah speaks to Job out of the storm; not, however, in wrath, but in the profound condescension of His majesty, in order to deliver His servant from dark imaginings, and to bring him to free and joyous knowledge. He does not demand blind subjection, but free submission; He does not extort an acknowledgement of His greatness, but it is effected by persuasion. It becomes manifest that God is much more forbearing and compassionate than men. Observe the friends, the defenders of the divine honour, these sticklers for their own orthodoxy, how they rave against Job! How much better is it to fall into the hands of the living God, than into the hands of man! For God is truth and love; but men have at one time love without truth, at another truth without love, since they either connive at one or anathematize him. When a man who, moreover, like Job, is a servant of God, fails in one point, or sins, men at once condemn him altogether, and admit nothing good in him; God, however, discerns between good and evil, and makes the good a means of freeing the man from the evil. He also does not go rashly to work, but waits, like an instructor, until the time of action arrives. How long He listens to Job’s bold challenging, and keeps silence! And then, when He does begin to speak, He does not cast Job to the ground by His authoritative utterances, but deals with him as a child; He examines him from the catechism of nature, and allows him to say for himself that he fails in this examination. In this second speech He acts with him as in the well-known poem of Hans Sachs with St. Peter: He offers him to take the government of the world for once instead of Himself. Here also He produces conviction; here also His mode of action is a deep lowering of Himself. It is Jehovah, the God, who at length begets Himself in humanity, in order to convince men of His love.
entries.c1b7e5a30b67ab8205c902d1515a3cf71bf270b1: <reference osisRef="Job.40.7-Job.9.7">Job 40:7-9   7</reference>  Gird up thy loins manfully: <div eID="gen8720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8721" type="x-p"/> I will question thee, and do thou answer me!   8  Wilt thou altogether annul my right, <div eID="gen8721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8722" type="x-p"/> Condemn me, that thou mayest be righteous?   9  And hast thou then an arm like God, <div eID="gen8722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8723" type="x-p"/> And canst thou with the voice thunder like Him? <div eID="gen8723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8724" type="x-p"/> The question with האף stands to <reference osisRef="Job.40.2">Job 40:2</reference> in the relation of a climax: Job contended not alone with God, which is in itself wrong, let it be whatsoever it may; he went so far as to lose sight of the divine justice in the government of the world, and in order not to be obliged to give up his own righteousness, so far as to doubt the divine. ואם, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.40.9">Job 40:9</reference></hi>, is also interrogative, as <reference osisRef="Job.8.3">Job 8:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.21.4">Job 21:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.34.17">Job 34:17</reference>, comp. <reference osisRef="Job.39.13">Job 39:13</reference>, not expressive of a wish, as Job 34:16. In the government of the world, God shows His arm, He raises His voice of thunder: canst thou perhaps - asks Jehovah - do the like, thou who seemest to imagine thou couldst govern the world more justly, if thou hadst to govern it? וּבקוּל כּמהוּ are to be combined: of like voice to Him; the translation follows the accents (ובקול with <hi type="italic">Rebia mugrasch</hi>).
entries.a07f68321bd2e9c7b973cc65276ec0f0888080ae: <reference osisRef="Job.40.10-Job.14.10">Job 40:10-14 10</reference>  Deck thyself then with pomp and dignity, <div eID="gen8724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8725" type="x-p"/> And in glory and majesty clothe thyself! 11  Let the overflowings of thy wrath pour forth, <div eID="gen8725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8726" type="x-p"/> And behold all pride, and abase it! 12  Behold all pride, bring it low, <div eID="gen8726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8727" type="x-p"/> And cast down the evil-doers in their place; 13  Hide them in the dust together, <div eID="gen8727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8728" type="x-p"/> Bind their faces in secret: 14  Then I also will praise thee, <div eID="gen8728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8729" type="x-p"/> That thy right hand obtaineth thee help. <div eID="gen8729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8730" type="x-p"/> He is for once to put on the robes of the King of kings (עדה, comp. עטח, to wrap round, <reference osisRef="Ps.104.2">Psa 104:2</reference>), and send forth his wrath over pride and evil-doing, for their complete removal. הפיץ, <hi type="italic">effundere, diffundere</hi>, as Arab. <hi type="italic">afâda</hi>, vid., Job 37:11. עברות, or rather, according to the reading of Ben-Ascher, עברות ,rehcsA, in its prop. signif. oversteppings, i.e., overflowings. In connection with <reference osisRef="Job.40.11">Job 40:11</reference>, one is directly reminded of the judgment on everything that is high and exalted in Isa 2, where beטמנם בּעפר also has its parallel (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.10">Isa 2:10</reference>). Not less, however, does <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.40.14">Job 40:14</reference></hi> recall <reference osisRef="Isa.59.16">Isa 59:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.63.5">Isa 63:5</reference> (comp. <reference osisRef="Ps.98.1">Psa 98:1</reference>); Isaiah I and II have similar descriptions to the book of Job. In connection with תמוּן (from טמן; Aram., Arab., טמר), the lower world, including the grave, is thought of (comp. Arab. <hi type="italic">mat - murât ,</hi> subterranean places); חבשׁ signifies, like Arab. <hi type="italic">ḥbs</hi> IV, to chain and to imprison. Try it only for once - this is the collective thought - to act like Me in the execution of penal justice, I would praise thee. entries.93adfe44da84e3494797a3e064cb6387e9bd9b51: <reference osisRef="Job.40.15-Job.18.15">Job 40:15-18 15</reference>  Behold now the behêmôth, <div eID="gen8730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8731" type="x-p"/> Which I have made with thee: <div eID="gen8731" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8732" type="x-p"/> He eateth grass like an ox. 16  Behold now, his strength is in his loins, <div eID="gen8732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8733" type="x-p"/> And his force in the sinews of his belly. 17  He bendeth his tail like a cedar branch, <div eID="gen8733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8734" type="x-p"/> The sinews of his legs are firmly interwoven. 18  His bones are like tubes of brass, <div eID="gen8734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8735" type="x-p"/> His bones like bars of iron. בּהמות (after the manner of the intensive <hi type="italic">plur</hi>. הוללות, חכמות, which play the part of the abstract termination), which sounds like a <hi type="italic">plur.,</hi> but without the numerical plural signification, considered as Hebrew, denotes the beast κατ ̓ ἐξοχήν, or the giant of beasts, is however Hebraized from the Egyptian <hi type="italic">p - ehe - mau</hi>, (<hi type="italic">muau</hi>), i.e., the (<hi type="italic">p</hi>) ox (<hi type="italic">ehe</hi>) of the water (<hi type="italic">mau</hi> as in the Hebraized proper name משׁה). It is, as Bochart has first of all shown, the so-called river or Nile horse, <hi type="italic">Hippopotamus amphibius</hi> (in <reference osisRef="Isa.30.6">Isa 30:6</reference>, בּהמות נגב, as emblem of Egypt, which extends its power, and still is active in the interest of others), found in the rivers of Africa, but no longer found in the Nile, which is not inappropriately called a horse; the Arab. water-hog is better, Italian <hi type="italic">bomarino,</hi> Eng. sea-cow ?, like the Egyptian <hi type="italic">p - ehe - mau</hi>. The change of <hi type="italic">p</hi> and <hi type="italic">b</hi> in the exchange of Egyptian and Semitic words occurs also elsewhere, e.g., <hi type="italic">pug'</hi> and בּוּץ, <hi type="italic">harpu</hi> and חרב (ἅρπη), <hi type="italic">Apriu</hi> and עברים (according to Lauth). Nevertheless <hi type="italic">p - ehe - mau</hi> (not <hi type="italic">mau - t</hi>, for what should the post-positive fem. art. do here?) is first of all only the בהמות translated back again into the Egyptian by Jablonsky; an instance in favour of this is still wanting. In Hieroglyph the Nile-horse is called <hi type="italic">apet ;</hi> it was honoured as divine. Brugsch dwelt in Thebes in the temple of the <hi type="italic">Apet.</hi><note placement="foot">In the astronomical representations the hippopotamus is in the neighbourhood of the North Pole in the place of the dragon of the present day, and bears the name of <hi type="italic">hes-mut</hi>, in which <hi type="italic">mut</hi> = <hi type="italic">t . mau ,</hi> “the mother.” <hi type="italic">Hes</hi> however is obscure; Birch explains it by: raging.</note> <div eID="gen8735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8736" type="x-p"/> In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.40.15">Job 40:15</reference></hi> עמּך signifies nothing but “with thee,” so that thou hast it before thee. This water-ox eats חציר, green grass, like an ox. That it prefers to plunder the produce of the fields - in Arab. <hi type="italic">chadı̂r</hi> signifies, in particular, green barley - is accordingly self-evident. Nevertheless, it has gigantic strength, viz., in its plump loins and in the sinews (שׁרירי, properly the firm constituent parts,<note placement="foot">Staring from its primary signification (made firm, fast), Arab. <hi type="italic">srı̂r</hi>, שׁרירא can signify e.g., also things put together from wood: a throne, a hand-barrow, bedstead and cradle, metaphor. the foundation. Wetzst. otherwise: “The שׂרירי הבטן are not the sinews and muscles, still less 'the private parts’ of others, but the four bearers of the animal body = <hi type="italic">arkân el - batn</hi>, viz., the bones of the מתנים, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.40.16">Job 40:16</reference></hi>, together with the two shoulder-blades. The Arab. <hi type="italic">sarı̂r</hi> is that on which a thing is supported or rests, on which it stands firmly, or moves about. <hi type="italic">Neshwân</hi> (i. 280) says: <hi type="italic">‛sarı̂r</hi> is the substratum on which a thing rests,' and the <hi type="italic">sarı̂r er - ra's</hi>, says the same, is the place where the head rests upon the nape of the neck. The <hi type="italic">Kâmûs</hi> gives the same signification <hi type="italic">primo loco</hi>, which shows that it is general; then follows in gen. Arab. <hi type="italic">muḍṭaja‛ ,</hi> “the support of a thing.”</note> therefore: ligaments and muscles) of its clumsy belly. The brush of a tail, short in comparison with the monster itself, is compared to a cedar (a branch of it), <hi type="italic">ratione glabritiei, rotunditatis, spissitudinis et firmitatis</hi> (Bochart); since the beast is in general almost without hair, it looks like a stiff, naked bone, and yet it can bend it like an elastic cedar branch; חפץ is Hebraeo-Arab., <hi type="italic">ḥfḍ</hi><note placement="foot">Wetzst. otherwise: One may compare the Arab. <hi type="italic">chafaḍa , fut. i,</hi> to hold, sit, lie motionless (in any place), from which the signification of desiring, longing, has been developed, since in the Semitic languages the figure of fixing (<hi type="italic">ta‛alluq</hi>) the heard and the eye on any desired object is at the basis of this notion (wherefore such verbs are joined with the <hi type="italic">praep</hi>. בּ). According to this, it is to be explained, “his tail is motionless like (the short and thick stem of) The cedar,” for the stunted tail of an animal is a mark of its strength to a Semite. In 1860, as I was visiting the neighbouring mountain fortress of <hi type="italic">el-Hosn</hi> with the octogenarian <hi type="italic">Fêjâd</hi>, the sheikh of <hi type="italic">Fîk</hi> in <hi type="italic">Gôlân</hi>, we rode past Fêjâd’s ploughmen; and as one of them was letting his team go slowly along, the sheikh cried out to him from a distance: Faster! faster! They (the steers, which thou ploughest) are not oxen weak with age, nor are they the dower of a widow (who at her second marriage receives only a pair of weak wretched oxen from her father or brother); but they are heifers (3-4 year-old steers) with stiffly raised tails (<hi type="italic">wadhujûluhin muqashmare</hi>, מקשׁמר an intensive קשׁוּר or שׁלאנן comp. שׁלאנן, <reference osisRef="Job.21.23">Job 21:23</reference>).</note> is a word used directly of the bending of wood (<hi type="italic">el - ‛ûd</hi>). <div eID="gen8736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8737" type="x-p"/> Since this description, like the whole book of Job, is so strongly Arabized, פחד, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.40.17">Job 40:17</reference></hi>, will also be one word with the Arab. <hi type="italic">fachidh</hi>, the thigh; as the Arabic version also translates: <hi type="italic">‛urûku afchâdhihi</hi> (the veins or strings of its thigh). The Targ., retaining the word of the text here,<note placement="foot">Another Targ., which translates גבריה ושׁעבוזוהי, <hi type="italic">penis et testiculi ejus</hi>, vid., Aruch <hi type="italic">s.v.</hi> שׁעבז.</note> has פּחדין in <reference osisRef="Lev.21.20">Lev 21:20</reference> for אשׁך, a testicle, prop. <hi type="italic">inguina</hi>, the groins; we interpret: the sinews of its thighs or legs<note placement="foot">According to Fleischer, <hi type="italic">fachidh</hi> signifies properly the thick-leg (= thigh), from the root <hi type="italic">fach</hi>, with the general signification of being puffed out, swollen, thick.</note> are intertwined after the manner of intertwined vine branches, שׂריגים.<note placement="foot">In the choice of the word ישׂרגו, the <hi type="italic">mushâgarat ed - dawâlı̂</hi> (from שׁגר = שׂרג), “the interweaving of the vine branches” was undoubtedly before the poet’s eye; comp. <hi type="italic">Deutsch. Morgenl. Zeitschr</hi>. xi. 477: “On all sides in this delightful corner of the earth (the <hi type="italic">Ghûta</hi>) the vine left to itself, in diversified ramifications, often a dozen branches resembling so many huge snakes entangled together, swings to and fro upon the shining stem of the lofty white poplar.” And <hi type="italic">ib</hi>. S. 491: “a twisted vine almost the thickness of a man, as though formed of rods of iron (comp. <reference osisRef="Job.40.18">Job 40:18</reference>).”</note> <div eID="gen8737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8738" type="x-p"/> But why is פחדיו pointed thus, and not פחדיו (as e.g., שׁעריו)? It is either an Aramaizing (with אשׁריו it has another relationship) pointing of the <hi type="italic">plur.,</hi> or rather, as Köhler has perceived, a regularly-pointed <hi type="italic">dual</hi> (like רגליו), from פּחדים (like פּעמים), which is equally suitable in connection with the signification <hi type="italic">femora</hi> as <hi type="italic">testiculi</hi>. מטיל, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.40.18">Job 40:18</reference></hi>, is also Hebraeo-Arab.; for Arab. <hi type="italic">mṭl</hi> signifies to forge, or properly to extend by forging (hammering), and to lengthen, undoubtedly a secondary formation of טוּל, <hi type="italic">tâla</hi>, to be long, as <hi type="italic">makuna</hi> of <hi type="italic">kâna</hi>, <hi type="italic">madana</hi> of <hi type="italic">dâna</hi>, <hi type="italic">massara</hi> (to found a fortified city) of <hi type="italic">sâra</hi>, chiefly (if not always) by the intervention of such nouns as <hi type="italic">makân , medı̂ne , misr</hi> (= מצור), therefore in the present instance by the intervention of this <hi type="italic">metı̂l</hi> (= <hi type="italic">memtûl</hi>)<note placement="foot">The noun מטיל is also found in the Lexicon of <hi type="italic">Neshwân</hi>, i. 63: “מטיל is equivalent to ממטוּל, viz., that which is hammered out in length, used of iron and other metals; and one says חדידה מטילה of a piece of iron that has been hammered for the purpose of stretching it.” The verb <hi type="italic">Neshwân</hi> explains: “מטל said of iron signifies to stretch it that it may become long.” The verb מטל can be regarded as a fusion of the root מדד (מטט, טוּט, comp. מוטה, and Arab. <hi type="italic">mûṭ</hi> Beduin: to take long steps) with the root טוּל, to be long. - Wetzst. The above explanation of the origin of the verb מטל seems to us more probable.</note> whence probably μέταλλον (metal), properly iron in bars or rods, therefore metal in a wrought state, although not yet finished.<note placement="foot">Ibn-Koreisch in Pinsker, <hi type="italic">Likkute</hi>, p. קנא, explains it without exactness by <hi type="italic">sebikat hadı̂d</hi>, which signifies a smelted and formed piece of iron.</note> <div eID="gen8738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8739" type="x-p"/> Its bones are like tubes of brass, its bones (גּרמיו, the more Aram. word) like forged rods of iron - what an appropriate description of the comparatively thin but firm as iron skeleton by which the plump mass of flesh of the gigantic boar-like grass-eater is carried!
entries.c59a54b0ccc180c72dfcf03b64843da99e33450b: <reference osisRef="Job.40.19-Job.24.19">Job 40:19-24 19</reference>  He is the firstling of the ways of God; <div eID="gen8739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8740" type="x-p"/> He, his Maker, reached to him his sword. 20  For the mountains bring forth food for him, <div eID="gen8740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8741" type="x-p"/> And all the beasts of the field play beside him. 21  Under the lote-trees he lieth down, <div eID="gen8741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8742" type="x-p"/> In covert of reeds and marsh. 22  Lote-trees cover him as shade, <div eID="gen8742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8743" type="x-p"/> The willows of the brook encompass him. 23  Behold, if the stream is strong, he doth not quake; <div eID="gen8743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8744" type="x-p"/> He remaineth cheerful, if a Jordan breaketh forth upon his mouth. 24  Just catch him while he is looking, <div eID="gen8744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8745" type="x-p"/> With snares let one pierce his nose! <div eID="gen8745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8746" type="x-p"/> God’s ways is the name given to God’s operations as the Creator of the world in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.40.19">Job 40:19</reference></hi> (comp. <reference osisRef="Job.26.14">Job 26:14</reference>, where His acts as the Ruler of the world are included); and the firstling of these ways is called the Behêmôth, not as one of the first in point of time, but one of the hugest creatures, <hi type="italic">un chef-d'oeuvre de Dieu</hi> (Bochart); ראשׁית not as <reference osisRef="Prov.8.22">Pro 8:22</reference>; Num 24:20, of the priority of time, but as <reference osisRef="Amos.6.1">Amo 6:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.6.6">Amo 6:6</reference>, of rank. The <hi type="italic">art</hi>. in העשׁו is, without the pronominal <hi type="italic">suff</hi>. being meant as an accusative (Ew. §290, <hi type="italic">d</hi>), equal to a demonstrative pronoun (comp. Ges. §109, <hi type="italic">init</hi>): this its Creator (but so that “this” does not refer back so much as forwards). It is not meant that He reached His sword to behêmoth, but (on which account לו is intentionally wanting) that He brought forth, i.e., created, its (behêmoth’s) peculiar sword, viz., the gigantic incisors ranged opposite one another, with which it grazes upon the meadow as with a sickle: ἀρούρῃσιν κακὴν ἐπιβάλλεται ἅρπην (Nicander, <hi type="italic">Theriac</hi>. 566), ἅρπη is exactly the sickle-shaped Egyptian sword (<hi type="italic">harpu</hi> = חרב). Vegetable food (to which its teeth are adapted) is appointed to the behêmoth: “for the mountains produce food for him;” it is the herbage of the hills (which is scanty in the lower and more abundant in the upper valley of the Nile) that is intended, after which this uncouth animal climbs (vid., Schlottm.). בּוּל is neither a contraction of יבוּל (Ges.), nor a corruption of it (Ew.), but Hebraeo-Arab. = <hi type="italic">baul</hi>, produce, from <hi type="italic">bâla</hi>, to beget, comp. <hi type="italic">aballa</hi>, to bear fruit (prop. seed, <hi type="italic">bulal</hi>), root בל, to soak, wet, mix.<note placement="foot">Whether בּליל, <reference osisRef="Job.6.5">Job 6:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.24.6">Job 24:6</reference>, signifies mixed provender (<hi type="italic">farrago</hi>), or perhaps ripe fruit, i.e., grain, so that <hi type="italic">jabol</hi>, Jdg 19:21, in the signification “he gave dry provender consisting of barley-grain,” would be the opposite of the <hi type="italic">jahushsh</hi> (יחשׁ) of the present day, “he gives green provender consisting of green grass or green barley, <hi type="italic">hashı̂sh</hi>,” as Wetzst. supposes, vid., on Isa 30:24.</note><hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.40.20">Job 40:20</reference></hi> describes how harmless, and if unmolested, inoffensive, the animal is; שׁם there, viz., while it is grazing. <div eID="gen8746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8747" type="x-p"/> In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.40.21">Job 40:21</reference></hi> Saadia correctly translates: Arab. <hi type="italic">tḥt 'l - ḍâl ;</hi> and <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.40.22">Job 40:22</reference></hi>, Abulwalid: Arab. <hi type="italic">ygṭı̂h 'l - ḍl mdlllâ lh , tegit eum lotus obumbrans eum,</hi> by interpreting Arab. <hi type="italic">'l - ḍl ,</hi> more correctly Arab. <hi type="italic">'l - ḍâl ,</hi> with <hi type="italic">es - sidr el - berrı̂ ,</hi> i.e., <hi type="italic">Rhamnus silvestris</hi> (<hi type="italic">Rhamnus Lotus,</hi> Linn.), in connection with which Schultens’ observation is to be noticed: <hi type="italic">Cave intelligas lotum Aegyptiam s. plantam Niloticam quam Arabes</hi> Arab. <hi type="italic">nûfr</hi>. The fact that the wild animals of the steppe seek the shade of the lote-tree, Schultens has supported by passages from the poets. The lotus is found not only in Syria, but also in Egypt, and the whole of Africa.<note placement="foot">The Arab. <hi type="italic">ḍâl</hi> or <hi type="italic">Dûm -</hi>tree, which likes hot and damp valleys, and hence is found much on the northern, and in great numbers on the eastern, shores of the Sea of Galilee, is called in the present day <hi type="italic">sidra</hi>, collect. <hi type="italic">sidr ;</hi> and its fruit, a small yellow apple, <hi type="italic">dûma</hi>, collect. <hi type="italic">dûm</hi>, perhaps “the not ending, perennial,” because the fruit of the previous year only falls from the tree when that of the present year is ripe. Around Bagdad, as they told me, the <hi type="italic">Dûm</hi>-tree bears twice a year. In Egypt its fruit is called <hi type="italic">nebq</hi> (נבק, not <hi type="italic">nibq</hi> as in Freytag), and the tree is there far stronger and taller than in Syria, where it is seldom more than about four and twenty feet high. Only in the <hi type="italic">Wâdi 's-sidr</hi> on the mountains of Judaea have I seen several unusually large trunks. The <hi type="italic">Kâmûs</hi> places the signification “the sweet <hi type="italic">Dûm</hi>-tree” first of all to Arab. <hi type="italic">ḍâl</hi>, and then “the wild D.” In hotter regions there may also be a superior kind with fine fruit, in Syria it is only wild - <hi type="italic">Neshwân</hi> (ii. 192) says: “<hi type="italic">dâla</hi>, collect. <hi type="italic">dâl</hi>, is the wild <hi type="italic">Dûm</hi>-tree,” - yet I have always found its fruit sweet and pleasant to the taste. - Wetzst.</note> <div eID="gen8747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8748" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">plur</hi>. is formed from the primary form צאל, as שׁקמים from שׁקם, Olsh. §148, <hi type="italic">b</hi>; the single tree was perhaps called צאלה (= Arab. <hi type="italic">ḍâlt</hi>), as שׁקמה (Ew. §189, <hi type="italic">h</hi>). Ammianus Marc. xxii. 15 coincides with <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.40.21">Job 40:21</reference></hi>: <hi type="italic">Inter arundines celsas et squalentes nimia densitate haec bellua cubilia ponit</hi>. צללו, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.40.22">Job 40:22</reference></hi> (resolved from צלּו, as גּללו, <reference osisRef="Job.20.7">Job 20:7</reference>, from גּלּו),<note placement="foot">Forms like גּלל, צלל, are unknown to the language, because it was more natural for ease of pronunciation to make the primary form סבבּ into סב than into סבב, גּללו (vid., p. 449), צללו, might more readily be referred to גּלל, צלל (in which the first <hi type="italic">a</hi> is a helping vowel, and the second a root vowel); but although the form קטל and the segolate forms completely pass into one another in inflection, still there does not exist a safe example in favour of the change of vowels of קטל into קטלי; wherefore we have also derived אגלי, <reference osisRef="Job.38.28">Job 38:28</reference>, from אגל, not from אגל, although, moreover, <hi type="italic">̇̇</hi> frequently enough alternates with <hi type="italic">̇̇</hi> (e.g., ישׁעך), and a transition into <hi type="italic">̇̇</hi> of the <hi type="italic">̇̇</hi> weakened from <hi type="italic">̇̇</hi> (e.g., ידכם) also occurs. But there are no forms like נטפי = נטפי from נטף in reality, although they would be possible according to the laws of vowels. In Ges. <hi type="italic">Handwörterb</hi>. (1863) גּללו stands under גּלל (according to the form לבב, which, however, forms לבבו) and צללו under סלל ( a rare noun-form, which does not occur at all from verbs double <hi type="italic">Ayin</hi>).</note> is in apposition with the subj.: Lote-trees cover it as its shade (shading it). The double play of words in <reference osisRef="Job.40.22">Job 40:22</reference> is not reproduced in the English translation. הן, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.40.23">Job 40:23</reference></hi>, pointing to something possible, obtains almost the signification of a conditional particle, as <reference osisRef="Job.12.14">Job 12:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.23.8">Job 23:8</reference>; Isa 54:15. The Arabic version appropriately translates Arab. <hi type="italic">'n ṭgâ 'l - nhr ,</hi> for Arab. <hi type="italic">ṭgâ</hi> denotes exactly like עשׁק, excessive, insolent behaviour, and is then, as also Arab. <hi type="italic">dlm , ‛tâ ,</hi> and other verbs given by Schultens, transferred from the sphere of ethics to the overflow of a river beyond its banks, to the rush of raging waters, to the rising and bursting forth of swollen streams. It does not, however, terrify the behêmoth, which can live as well in the water as on the land; לא יחפּוז, properly, it does not spring up before it, is not disturbed by it. Instead of the Jordan, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.40.23">Job 40:23</reference></hi>, especially in connection with יגיח, the <hi type="italic">'Gaihûn</hi> (the Oxus) or the <hi type="italic">'Gaihân</hi> (the Pyramus) might have been mentioned, which have their names from the growing force with which they burst forth from their sources (גּיח, גּוּח, comp. <hi type="italic">'gâcha ,</hi> to wash away). But in order to express the notion of a powerful and at times deep-swelling stream, the poet prefers the ירדּן of his fatherland, which moreover, does not lie so very far from the scene, according to the conception at least, since all the wadis in its neighbourhood flow directly or indirectly (as <hi type="italic">Wâdi el-Meddân,</hi> the boundary river between the district of <hi type="italic">Suwêt</hi> and the <hi type="italic">Nukra</hi> plain) into the Jordan. For ירדּן (perhaps from ירד)<note placement="foot">Certainly one would have expected ירדּן like גּרזן, while ירדּן like יעבּץ, יעזר, appears formed from רדן; nevertheless ירדּן (with changeable <hi type="italic">Ssere</hi>) can be understood as a change of vowel from ירדּן (comp. ישׁב for ישׁב).</note> does not here signify a stream (rising in the mountain) in general; the name is not deprived of its geographical definiteness, but is a particularizing expression of the notion given above. <div eID="gen8748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8749" type="x-p"/> The description closes in <reference osisRef="Job.40.24">Job 40:24</reference> with the ironical challenge: in its sight (בּעיניו as <reference osisRef="Prov.1.17">Pro 1:17</reference>) let one (for once) catch it; let one lay a snare which, when it goes into it, shall spring together and pierce it in the nose; i.e., neither the open force nor the stratagem, which one employs with effect with other animals, is sufficient to overpower this monster. מוקשׁים is generally rendered as equal to חחים, <reference osisRef="Isa.37.29">Isa 37:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.19.4">Eze 19:4</reference>, or at least to the cords drawn through them, but contrary to the uniform usage of the language. The description of the hippopotamus<note placement="foot">Vid., Grehm, <hi type="italic">Aus dem Leben des Nilpferds, Gartenlaube</hi> 1859, Nr. 48, etc.</note> is not followed by that of the crocodile, which also elsewhere form a pair, e.g., in Achilles Tatius, iv. 2, 19. Behemoth and leviathan, says Herder, are the pillars of Hercules at the end of the book, the <hi type="italic">non plus ultra</hi> of another world distant from the scene. What the same writer says of the poet, that he does not “mean to furnish any contributions to Pennant’s <hi type="italic">Zoologie</hi> or to Linnaeus’ <hi type="italic">Animal Kingdom</hi>,” the expositor also must assent to.  <chapter eID="Job.40"/> <div eID="gen8749" type="x-p"/>
